label: Action theory (philosophy)

label: Ad hoc hypothesis

label: Correspondence theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Correspondence theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In metaphysics and philosophy of language, the correspondence theory of truth states that the truth or falsity of a statement is determined only by how it relates to the world and whether it accurately describes (i.e., corresponds with) that world.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Correspondence theory of truth

label: Availability cascade
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Availability cascade", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An availability cascade is a self-reinforcing cycle that explains the development of certain kinds of collective beliefs.

label: Critical thinking
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Critical thinking", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Critical thinking is the process of analyzing available facts, evidence, observations, and arguments to reach sound conclusions or informed choices.

label: Informal fallacy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Informal fallacy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Informal fallacies are a type of incorrect argument in natural language.

label: Formal fallacy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Formal fallacy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In logic and philosophy, a formal fallacy is a pattern of reasoning with a flaw in its logical structure (the logical relationship between the premises and the conclusion).

label: Skepticism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Skepticism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Skepticism (US) or scepticism (UK) is a questioning attitude or doubt toward knowledge claims that are seen as mere belief or dogma.

label: Absoluteness (logic)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Absoluteness (logic)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematical logic, a formula is said to be absolute to some class of structures (also called models), if it has the same truth value in each of the members of that class.

label: Philosophical logic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Philosophical logic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Understood in a narrow sense, philosophical logic is the area of logic that studies the application of logical methods to philosophical problems, often in the form of extended logical systems like modal logic.

label: Adverse inference
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Adverse inference", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Adverse inference is a legal inference, adverse to the concerned party, drawn from silence or absence of requested evidence.

label: Candle problem
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Candle problem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The candle problem or candle task, also known as Duncker's candle problem, is a cognitive performance test, measuring the influence of functional fixedness on a participant's problem solving capabilities.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense is a logical argument developed by the American analytic philosopher Alvin Plantinga and published in its final version in his 1977 book God, Freedom, and Evil.

label: A series and B series
summary: English Wikipedia (article "A series and B series", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In metaphysics, the A series and the B series are two different descriptions of the temporal ordering relation among events.

label: Measurement
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Measurement", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Measurement is the quantification of attributes of an object or event, which can be used to compare with other objects or events.

label: Cognitive bias
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cognitive bias", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from the norm or rationality in judgment.

label: Pseudoscience
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Pseudoscience", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Pseudoscience consists of statements, beliefs, or practices that claim to be scientific but are inherently incompatible with the scientific method.

label: A priori and a posteriori
summary: English Wikipedia (article "A priori and a posteriori", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In epistemology, a priori (‘from the earlier’) and a posteriori (‘from the later’) are the two categories of knowledge, justification, or argument, determining whether or not a proposition is reliant on outside sensory experience.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "History and philosophy of science", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The history and philosophy of science (HPS) is an academic discipline that encompasses the history of science and the philosophy of science.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "B-theory of time", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The B-theory of time, also called the tenseless theory of time, is one of two positions regarding the temporal ordering of events in the philosophy of time.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: B-theory of time

label: Deflationary theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Deflationary theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy and logic, a deflationary theory of truth (also semantic deflationism or simply deflationism) is one of a family of theories that all have in common the claim that assertions of predicate truth of a statement do not attribute a property called "truth" to such a statement.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Deflationary theory of truth

label: Archival research
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Archival research", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Archival research is a type of research which involves seeking out and extracting evidence from archival records.

label: Agent causation
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Agent causation", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Agent causation (or agent causality) is a category of determination in metaphysics, where a being who is not an event—namely an agent—can cause events (particularly the agent's own actions).

label: Adaptive reasoning
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Adaptive reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Adaptive reasoning refers to a problem solving strategy that adapts thinking to address a problem as it changes and evolves.

label: Affirming the consequent
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Affirming the consequent", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In propositional logic, affirming the consequent (also known as converse error, fallacy of the converse, or confusion of necessity and sufficiency) is a formal fallacy (or an invalid form of argument) that is committed when, in the context of an indicative conditional statement, it is stated that because the consequent is true, therefore the antecedent is true.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Affirming the consequent

label: Empiric school
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Empiric school", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The Empiric school of medicine (Empirics, Empiricists, or Empirici, Greek: Ἐμπειρικοί) was a school of medicine founded in Alexandria the middle of the third century BC.

label: Cartesianism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cartesianism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Cartesianism is the philosophical and scientific system of René Descartes and its subsequent development by other seventeenth century thinkers, most notably François Poullain de la Barre, Nicolas Malebranche and Baruch Spinoza.

label: Accident (philosophy)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Accident (philosophy)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An accident (Greek συμβεβηκός), in metaphysics and philosophy, is a property that the entity or substance has contingently, without which the substance can still retain its identity.

label: Agentive logic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Agentive logic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Agentive logic (also called the logic of action or logic of agency) is the field of philosophical logic and logic in computer science that studies formal representations of agents, their actions, and their abilities.

label: Catch-22 (logic)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Catch-22 (logic)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A catch-22 is a paradoxical situation from which an individual cannot escape because of contradictory rules or limitations.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Arbitrary inference", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Arbitrary inference is a classic tenet of cognitive therapy created by Aaron T. Beck in 1979.

label: Analogy

label: Absolute (philosophy)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Absolute (philosophy)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy (often specifically metaphysics), the absolute, in most common usage, is an absolute perfect, self-sufficient reality that depends upon nothing external to itself.

label: Cognitive justice
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cognitive justice", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The concept of cognitive justice is based on the recognition of the plurality of knowledge and expresses the right of the different forms of knowledge to co-exist.

label: Admissible heuristic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Admissible heuristic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In computer science, specifically in algorithms related to pathfinding, a heuristic function is said to be admissible if it never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal, i.e. the cost it estimates to reach the goal is not higher than the lowest possible cost from the current point in the path.

label: Alphabet of human thought
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Alphabet of human thought", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The alphabet of human thought (Latin: alphabetum cogitationum humanarum) is a concept originally proposed by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz that provides a universal way to represent and analyze ideas and relationships by breaking down their component pieces.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Alphabet of human thought

label: Abductive reasoning
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Abductive reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Abductive reasoning (also called abduction, abductive inference, or retroduction) is a form of logical inference that seeks the simplest and most likely conclusion from a set of observations.

label: Bayesian epistemology
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bayesian epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Bayesian epistemology is a formal approach to various topics in epistemology that has its roots in Thomas Bayes' work in the field of probability theory.

label: Actor–network theory
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Actor–network theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Actor–network theory (ANT) is a theoretical and methodological approach to social theory where everything in the social and natural worlds exists in constantly shifting networks of relationships.

label: Argument from analogy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argument from analogy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Argument from analogy is a special type of inductive argument, where perceived similarities are used as a basis to infer some further similarity that has not been observed yet.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Argument from analogy

label: Ad personam
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ad personam", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In an argument, ad personam, short for argumentum ad personam, is a tactic aimed at discrediting one's opponent by attacking their personality, unrelated to the substance of the debate.

label: Denying the antecedent
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Denying the antecedent", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Denying the antecedent (also known as denial of the antecedent, inverse error, or fallacy of the inverse) is a formal fallacy of inferring the inverse from an original statement.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Denying the antecedent

label: Antinomy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Antinomy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy, an antinomy (; Ancient Greek: antí 'against' + nómos 'law') is a real or apparent contradiction between two conclusions, both of which seem justified.

label: Communicative rationality
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Communicative rationality", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Communicative rationality or communicative reason (German: kommunikative Rationalität) is a theory or set of theories which describes human rationality as a necessary outcome of successful communication.

label: Analogy of the divided line
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Analogy of the divided line", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The analogy of the divided line (Ancient Greek: γραμμὴ δίχα τετμημένη, romanized: grammē dicha tetmēmenē) is presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in the Republic (509d–511e).

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Analogy of the divided line

label: AI trust paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "AI trust paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The AI trust paradox (also known as the verisimilitude paradox) is the phenomenon where advanced artificial intelligence models become so proficient at mimicking human-like language and behavior that users increasingly struggle to determine if the information generated is accurate or simply plausible.

label: Absolute space and time
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Absolute space and time", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Absolute space and time is a concept in physics and philosophy about the properties of the universe.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Effective theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In science, an effective theory is a deliberately limited scientific theory applicable under specific circumstances.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Affect heuristic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The affect heuristic is a heuristic, a mental shortcut that allows people to make decisions and solve problems quickly and efficiently, in which current emotion—fear, pleasure, surprise, etc.—influences decisions.

label: Academic skepticism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Academic skepticism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Academic skepticism was the philosophy of the skeptical period of the Academy dating from around 266 BC, when Arcesilaus became scholarch, until around 90 BC, when Antiochus of Ascalon rejected skepticism, although individual philosophers, such as Favorinus and his teacher Plutarch, continued to defend skepticism after this date.

label: Abstraction
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Abstraction", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Abstraction is the process of generalizing rules and concepts from specific examples, literal (real or concrete) signifiers, first principles, or other methods.

label: Black swan theory
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Black swan theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The black swan theory or theory of black swan events is a metaphor that describes an event that comes as a surprise, has a major effect, and is often inappropriately rationalized after the fact with the benefit of hindsight.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Closed circle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A closed-circle argument is one that is unfalsifiable.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Epistemic theories of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy and epistemology, epistemic theories of truth are attempts to analyze the notion of truth in terms of epistemic notions such as knowledge, belief, acceptance, verification, justification, and perspective.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Analytic reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Analytical reasoning, also known as analytical thinking, refers to the ability to look at information, be it qualitative or quantitative in nature, and discern patterns within the information.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ecological fallacy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An ecological fallacy (also ecological inference fallacy or population fallacy) is a formal fallacy in the interpretation of statistical data that occurs when inferences about the nature of individuals are deduced from inferences about the group to which those individuals belong. "Ecological fallacy" is a term that is sometimes used to describe the fallacy of division, which is not a statistical fallacy.

label: Argumentation theory
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argumentation theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Argumentation theory is the interdisciplinary study of how conclusions can be supported or undermined by premises through logical reasoning.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ariadne's thread (logic)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Ariadne's thread, named for the legend of Ariadne who gave Theseus a ball of thread (literally a “clue”) to find his way back out of the Minotaur’s labyrinth, is solving a problem which has multiple apparent ways to proceed—such as a physical maze, a logic puzzle, or an ethical dilemma—through an exhaustive application of logic to all available routes.

label: Local skepticism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Local skepticism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Local skepticism is the view that one cannot possess knowledge in some particular domain.

label: Empirical evidence
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Empirical evidence", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Empirical evidence is evidence obtained through sense experience or experimental procedure.

label: Apodicticity
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Apodicticity", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: "Apodictic", also spelled "apodeictic" (Ancient Greek: ἀποδεικτικός, "capable of demonstration"), is an adjectival expression from Aristotelian logic that refers to propositions that are demonstrably, necessarily or self-evidently true.

label: Design rationale
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Design rationale", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A design rationale is an explicit documentation of the reasons behind decisions made when designing a system or artifact.

label: A/B testing
summary: English Wikipedia (article "A/B testing", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A/B testing (also known as bucket testing, split-run testing or split testing) is a user-experience research method.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Baconian method", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The Baconian method is the investigative method developed by Francis Bacon, one of the founders of modern science, and thus a first formulation of a modern scientific method.

label: Argument
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argument", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An argument is one or more premises—sentences, statements, or propositions—directed towards arriving at a logical conclusion.

label: Causal inference
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Causal inference", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Causal inference is the process of determining the independent, actual effect of a particular phenomenon that is a component of a larger system.

label: Appeal to the law
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Appeal to the law", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An appeal to the law (argumentum ad legem in Latin) is an informal fallacy in which someone tries to encourage or defend an action based on its legality, or condemn it as morally reprehensible, purely because it is illegal.

label: Distinction bias
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Distinction bias", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Distinction bias, a concept of decision theory, is the tendency to view two options as more distinctive when evaluating them simultaneously than when evaluating them separately.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argumentum a fortiori", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Argumentum a fortiori (literally "argument from the stronger [reason]") (UK: , US: ) is a form of argumentation that draws upon existing confidence in a proposition to argue in favour of a second proposition that is held to be implicit in, or even more certain than, the first.

label: Reasonable doubt
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Reasonable doubt", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Beyond (a) reasonable doubt is a legal standard of proof required to reach a criminal conviction in some adversarial legal systems.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Apophantic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In logic, Apophantic (Greek: ἀποφαντικός, "declaratory", from ἀποφαίνειν apophainein, "to show, to make known") statements are declaratory statements whose truth-value can be determined by examining whether its predicate can be logically attributed to its subject.

label: Dogma
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Dogma", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Dogma, in its broadest sense, is any belief held definitively and without the possibility of reform.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Data universalism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Data universalism is an epistemological framework that assumes a single universal narrative of any dataset without any consideration of geographical borders and social contexts.

label: Alethiology

label: Encyclopedic knowledge
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Encyclopedic knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: To have encyclopedic knowledge is to have "vast and complete" knowledge about a large number of diverse subjects.

label: Backward chaining
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Backward chaining", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Backward chaining (or backward reasoning) is an inference method described colloquially as working backward from the goal.

label: Differential effects

label: Argument from incredulity
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argument from incredulity", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Argument from incredulity, also known as argument from personal incredulity, appeal to common sense, or the divine fallacy, is a fallacy in informal logic.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Decolonization of knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Decolonization of knowledge (also epistemic decolonization or epistemological decolonization) is a concept advanced in decolonial scholarship that critiques the perceived hegemony of Western knowledge systems.

label: Further research is needed
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Further research is needed", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: "Further research is needed" (FRIN), "more research is needed" and other variants of similar phrases are commonly used in research papers.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Further research is needed

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Analysis of competing hypotheses", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The analysis of competing hypotheses (ACH) is a methodology for evaluating multiple competing hypotheses for observed data.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Autonomy of syntax", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In linguistics, the autonomy of syntax is the assumption that syntax is arbitrary and self-contained with respect to meaning: semantics, pragmatics, discourse function, and other factors external to language.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Autonomy of syntax

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Android epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Android epistemology is an approach to epistemology considering the space of possible machines and their capacities for knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, desires and for action in accord with their mental states.

label: Always already
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Always already", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy, always already describes the perception of phenomena by the mind of an observer.

label: Coherence theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Coherence theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In epistemology, the coherence theory of truth is a family of philosophical theories that characterize truth as a property of whole systems of propositions that can be ascribed to individual propositions only derivatively according to their coherence with the whole.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Coherence theory of truth

label: Antireductionism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Antireductionism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Antireductionism is the position in science and metaphysics that stands in contrast to reductionism (anti-holism) by advocating that not all properties of a system can be explained in terms of its constituent parts and their interactions.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Clinical study design", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Clinical study design is the formulation of clinical trials and other experiments, as well as observational studies, in medical research involving human beings and involving clinical aspects, including epidemiology .

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Both/and reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Both/and is an academic concept which refers to a form of reasoning which resists binary or either/or styles of thinking.

label: Argumentum ad baculum
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argumentum ad baculum", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Argumentum ad baculum (Latin for "argument to the cudgel" or "appeal to the stick") is a type of argument made when one attempts to appeal to force to bring about the acceptance of a conclusion.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Argumentum ad baculum

label: Inventor's paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Inventor's paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The inventor's paradox is a phenomenon that occurs in seeking a solution to a given problem.

label: Canberra Plan

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Axiom of reducibility", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The axiom of reducibility was introduced by Bertrand Russell in the early 20th century as part of his ramified theory of types.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Axiom of reducibility

label: Circular definition
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Circular definition", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A circular definition is a type of definition that uses the term(s) being defined as part of the description or assumes that the term(s) being described are already known.

label: Defeasibility (linguistics)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Defeasibility (linguistics)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the linguistic field of pragmatics, an inference is said to be defeasible or cancellable if it can be made to disappear by the addition of another statement, or an appropriate context.

label: Blockhead (thought experiment)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Blockhead (thought experiment)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Blockhead is a theoretical computer system invented as part of a thought experiment by philosopher Ned Block, which appeared in a paper titled "Psychologism and Behaviorism".

label: Bentley's paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bentley's paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In cosmology, Bentley's paradox, also known as Seeliger's paradox, Bentley–Seeliger paradox or Neumann–Seeliger paradox points to a problem occurring when Newton's theory of gravitation is applied to the universe.

label: Ecology of contexts
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ecology of contexts", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The ecology of contexts is a term used in many disciplines and refers to the dynamic interplay of contexts and demands that constrain and define an entity.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Ecology of contexts

label: Adaptive bias
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Adaptive bias", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Adaptive bias is the idea that the human brain has evolved to reason adaptively, rather than truthfully or even rationally, and that cognitive bias may have evolved as a mechanism to reduce the overall cost of cognitive errors as opposed to merely reducing the number of cognitive errors, when faced with making a decision under conditions of uncertainty.

label: Consistent heuristic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Consistent heuristic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the study of path-finding problems in artificial intelligence, a heuristic function is said to be consistent, or monotone, if its estimate is always less than or equal to the estimated distance from any neighbouring vertex to the goal, plus the cost of reaching that neighbour.

label: Anfinsen's dogma
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Anfinsen's dogma", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Anfinsen's dogma, also known as the thermodynamic hypothesis, is a postulate in molecular biology.

label: Ambiguity
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ambiguity", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Ambiguity, is a state in which the meaning of a phrase, statement, situation, or resolution is not explicitly defined, making for several plausible interpretations.

label: Coherentism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Coherentism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In epistemology, there are two types of coherentism: the coherence theory of truth, and the coherence theory of justification (also known as epistemic coherentism).

label: Antiscience
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Antiscience", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Antiscience is a set of attitudes and a form of anti-intellectualism that involves a rejection of science and the scientific method.

label: Epistemological rupture
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Epistemological rupture", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Epistemological rupture (or epistemological break) is a notion introduced in 1938 by French philosopher Gaston Bachelard, and later used by Louis Althusser.

label: Pragmatic theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Pragmatic theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A pragmatic theory of truth is a theory of truth within the philosophies of pragmatism and pragmaticism.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Pragmatic theory of truth

label: Causal closure
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Causal closure", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Physical causal closure is a metaphysical theory about the nature of causation in the physical realm with significant ramifications in the study of metaphysics and the mind.

label: Explicit knowledge
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Explicit knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Explicit knowledge (also expressive knowledge) is knowledge that can be readily articulated, conceptualized, codified, formalized, stored and accessed.

label: Cognitive dissonance
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cognitive dissonance", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the field of psychology, cognitive dissonance is described as a mental phenomenon in which people unknowingly or subconsciously hold fundamentally conflicting cognitions.

label: Case-based reasoning
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Case-based reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Case-based reasoning (CBR), broadly construed, is the process of solving new problems based on the solutions of similar past problems.

label: Generalization
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Generalization", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A generalization is a form of abstraction whereby common properties of specific instances are formulated as general concepts or claims.

label: Argumentum ad captandum
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Argumentum ad captandum", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In rhetoric, an argumentum ad captandum, "for capturing" the gullibility of the naïve among the listeners or readers, is an unsound, specious argument designed to appeal to the emotions rather than to the mind.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Argumentum ad captandum

label: Computational philosophy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Computational philosophy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Computational philosophy or digital philosophy is the use of computational techniques in philosophy.

label: Calculus ratiocinator
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Calculus ratiocinator", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The calculus ratiocinator is a theoretical universal logical calculation framework, a concept described in the writings of Gottfried Leibniz, usually paired with his more frequently mentioned characteristica universalis, a universal conceptual language.

label: Issue-based information system
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Issue-based information system", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The issue-based information system (IBIS) is an argumentation-based approach to clarifying wicked problems—complex, ill-defined problems that involve multiple stakeholders.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Issue-based information system

label: Epistemic democracy
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Epistemic democracy", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Epistemic democracy refers to a range of views in political science and philosophy which see the value of democracy as based, at least in part, on its ability to make good or correct decisions.

label: Additive bias
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Additive bias", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Additive bias is a cognitive urge or tendency of human beings facing problems to add resources instead of taking or subtracting.

label: Constructive heuristic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Constructive heuristic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A constructive heuristic is a type of heuristic method which starts with an empty solution and repeatedly extends the current solution until a complete solution is obtained.

label: Chronotope
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chronotope", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In literary theory and philosophy of language, the chronotope is how configurations of time and space are represented in language and discourse.

label: Appeal to the stone
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Appeal to the stone", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Appeal to the stone, also known as argumentum ad lapidem, is a logical fallacy that dismisses an argument as untrue or absurd.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Appeal to the stone

label: Analytic–synthetic distinction
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Analytic–synthetic distinction", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The analytic–synthetic distinction is a semantic distinction used primarily in philosophy to distinguish between propositions (in particular, statements that are affirmative subject–predicate judgments) that are of two types: analytic propositions and synthetic propositions.

label: Conciliationism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Conciliationism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Conciliationism is a view in the epistemology of disagreement according to which one should revise one's opinions closer to one's epistemic peers in the face of epistemic disagreement.

label: Explanatory power
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Explanatory power", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Explanatory power is the ability of a hypothesis or theory to explain the subject matter effectively to which it pertains.

label: Redundancy theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Redundancy theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: According to the redundancy theory of truth (also known as the disquotational theory of truth), asserting that a statement is true is completely equivalent to asserting the statement itself.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Redundancy theory of truth

label: Cross impact analysis
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cross impact analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Cross-impact analysis is a methodology developed by Theodore J. Gordon and Olaf Helmer in 1966 to help determine how relationships between events would impact resulting events and reduce uncertainty in the future.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Cross impact analysis

label: Forbidden knowledge
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Forbidden knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Forbidden knowledge is information, sometimes in the form of forbidden books, to which access is restricted or deprecated for political or religious reasons.

label: Communal reinforcement
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Communal reinforcement", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Communal reinforcement is a social phenomenon in which a concept or idea is repeatedly asserted in a community, regardless of whether sufficient empirical evidence has been presented to support it.

label: Causal reasoning
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Causal reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Causal reasoning is the process of identifying causality: the relationship between a cause and its effect.

label: Imperfect induction
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Imperfect induction", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Imperfect induction is the process of inferring from a sample of a group to what is characteristic of the whole group.

label: Conceptual engineering
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Conceptual engineering", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Conceptual engineering is a field in analytic philosophy that focuses on how to best assess and improve our conceptual schemes and repertoires.

label: Experiment
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Experiment", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: An experiment is a procedure carried out to support or refute a hypothesis, or determine the efficacy or likelihood of something previously untried.

label: Braitenberg vehicle
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Braitenberg vehicle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A Braitenberg vehicle is an imaginary robot or creature used as the subject of a thought experiment to study embodied cognition.

label: Chinese room
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chinese room", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The Chinese room argument holds that a computer executing a program cannot have a mind, understanding, or consciousness, regardless of how intelligently or human-like the program may make the computer behave.

label: Bracketing paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bracketing paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In linguistic morphology, the bracketing paradox concerns morphologically complex words which have more than one analysis, or bracketing, e.g., one for phonology and one for semantics, and the two are not compatible, or brackets do not align.

label: Aesthetic–usability effect
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Aesthetic–usability effect", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The aesthetic–usability effect describes a paradox that people perceive more aesthetic designs as much more intuitive than those considered to be less aesthetically pleasing.

label: Contagion heuristic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Contagion heuristic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The contagion heuristic is a psychological heuristic which follows the law of contagion and the law of similarity, leading people to avoid contact with people or objects viewed as "contaminated" by previous contact with someone or something viewed as bad—or, less often, to seek contact with objects that have been in contact with people or things considered good.

label: Access Consciousness
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Access Consciousness", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Access Consciousness is a pseudoscientific New Age movement founded by Gary Douglas in 1990 in Santa Barbara, California, initially called Access Energy Transformation.

label: Augustinian hypothesis
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Augustinian hypothesis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The Augustinian hypothesis (sometimes referred to as the Augustinian Proposal) is a solution to the synoptic problem, which concerns the origin of the canonical Gospels in the New Testament.

label: Code-talker paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Code-talker paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A code-talker paradox is a situation in which a language prevents communication.

label: Applied epistemology
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Applied epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Applied epistemology refers to the study that determines whether the systems of investigation that seek the truth lead to true beliefs about the world.

label: Anthropic principle
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Anthropic principle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In cosmology and philosophy of science, the anthropic principle (also known as the observation selection effect) is the proposition that the range of possible observations made about a universe is limited by the fact that observations can only be made if that universe is capable of developing observers in the first place.

label: Constructivism (philosophy of science)
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Constructivism (philosophy of science)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Constructionism is a view in the philosophy of science that maintains that scientific knowledge is constructed by the scientific community, which seeks to measure and construct models of the natural world.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Constructivism (philosophy of science)

summary: English Wikipedia (article "First principle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy and science, a first principle is a basic proposition or assumption that cannot be deduced from any other proposition or assumption.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Inductionism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Inductionism is the scientific philosophy where laws are "induced" from sets of data.

label: Dilemma

label: Instrumentalism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Instrumentalism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In philosophy of science and in epistemology, instrumentalism is a methodological view that ideas are useful instruments, and that the worth of an idea is based on how effective it is in explaining and predicting natural phenomena.

label: Canonical form
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Canonical form", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics and computer science, a canonical, normal, or standard form of a mathematical object is a standard way of presenting that object as a mathematical expression.

label: Compossibility
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Compossibility", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Compossibility is a philosophical concept from Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

label: Allegory of the cave
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Allegory of the cave", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The allegory of the cave is an allegory presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in his work Republic (514a–520a, Book VII) to compare "the effect of education (παιδεία) and the lack of it on our nature".

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Allegory of the cave

label: Feminist epistemology
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Feminist epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Feminist epistemology is an examination of epistemology from a feminist standpoint.

label: Apriorism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Apriorism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Apriorism (sometimes a priorism or a-priorism) in modern times, refers to epistemological positions that assume that certain knowledge can be justified without reference to experience, or, in a narrower sense, that knowledge is entirely possible without any experience.

label: Apperception
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Apperception", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Apperception (from the Latin ad-, "to, toward" and percipere, "to perceive, gain, secure, learn, or feel") is any of several aspects of perception and consciousness in such fields as psychology, philosophy and epistemology.

label: Contrastivism
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Contrastivism", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Contrastivism, or the contrast theory of meaning, is an epistemological theory proposed by Jonathan Schaffer that suggests that knowledge attributions have a ternary structure of the form 'S knows that p rather than q'.

label: Gestell
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Gestell", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Gestell (or Ge-stell, translated as "Enframing" or "positioning") is a German word used by twentieth-century German philosopher Martin Heidegger to describe what lies behind or beneath modern technology.

label: Semantic theory of truth
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Semantic theory of truth", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A semantic theory of truth is a theory of truth in the philosophy of language which holds that truth is a property of sentences.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Semantic theory of truth

label: Data sharing
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Data sharing", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Data sharing denotes the dissemination of research datasets to enable access and use by other investigators.

label: General knowledge
summary: English Wikipedia (article "General knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: General knowledge is information that has been accumulated over time through various media and sources.

label: Credulity
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Credulity", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Credulity is a person's willingness or ability to believe that a statement is true, especially on minimal or uncertain evidence.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Circumstantial evidence", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Circumstantial evidence is evidence that relies on an inference to connect it to a conclusion of fact, such as a fingerprint at the scene of a crime.

label: Begging the question
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Begging the question", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In classical rhetoric and logic, begging the question (Latin: petitio principii), or assuming the conclusion, is an informal fallacy that occurs when an argument's premises assume the truth of the conclusion.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Thought experiment", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A thought experiment is an imaginary scenario that is meant to elucidate or test an argument or theory.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Diairesis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Diairesis (Ancient Greek: διαίρεσις, romanized: diaíresis, "division") is a form of classification used in ancient (especially Platonic) logic that serves to systematize concepts and come to definitions.

label: Conditional logic
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Conditional logic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Conditional logic (also: the logic of conditionals) refers to a family of formal systems for reasoning with statements of the form "if A, (then) B".

label: Virtue epistemology
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Virtue epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Virtue epistemology is a philosophical approach to epistemology that stresses the importance of intellectual and specifically epistemic virtues.

label: Genetic epistemology
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Genetic epistemology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Genetic epistemology or 'developmental theory of knowledge' is a study of the origins (genesis) of knowledge (epistemology) established by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget.

label: Ambiguity effect
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ambiguity effect", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The ambiguity effect is a cognitive tendency where decision making is affected by a lack of information, or "ambiguity".

label: Action type approach
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Action type approach", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The action type approach is a series of mental exercises—variously described as "pseudoscientific", "empirically challenged", or a "neuromyth"— that purport to increase physical performance in athletes.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Action type approach

label: Concept horse paradox
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Concept horse paradox", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The concept "horse" paradox (also known as the concept horse problem or Frege's concept horse paradox; German: der Begriff Pferd) is a problem in the philosophy of language and philosophy of logic arising from Gottlob Frege's distinction between concept and object.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Concept horse paradox

label: Aristotle's theory of universals
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Aristotle's theory of universals", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Aristotle's theory of universals is Aristotle's classical solution to the problem of universals, sometimes known as the hylomorphic theory of immanent realism.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Aristotle's theory of universals

label: Appropriation of knowledge
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Appropriation of knowledge", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Appropriation of knowledge is the process of constructing knowledge from social and cultural sources, and integrating it into pre-existing schemas.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Appropriation of knowledge

label: Tarski's undefinability theorem
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Tarski's undefinability theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Tarski's undefinability theorem, stated and proved by Alfred Tarski in 1933, is an important limitative result in mathematical logic, the foundations of mathematics, and in formal semantics.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Tarski's undefinability theorem

label: Discovery science
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Discovery science", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Discovery science (also known as discovery-based science) is a scientific methodology which aims to find new patterns, correlations, and form hypotheses through the analysis of large-scale experimental data.

label: Causal theory of reference
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Causal theory of reference", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A causal theory of reference or historical chain theory of reference is a theory of how terms acquire specific referents based on evidence.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Causal theory of reference

label: Delusion
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Delusion", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A delusion is a fixed belief that is not amenable to change in light of conflicting evidence.

label: Commonsense reasoning
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Commonsense reasoning", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In artificial intelligence (AI), commonsense reasoning is a human-like ability to make presumptions about the type and essence of ordinary situations humans encounter every day.

summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cartesian circle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The Cartesian circle (also known as Arnauld's circle) is an example of fallacious circular reasoning attributed to French philosopher René Descartes.

label: Closed concept
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Closed concept", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A closed concept is a concept where all the necessary and sufficient conditions required to include something within the concept can be listed.

label: Contra principia negantem non est disputandum
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Contra principia negantem non est disputandum", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Contra principia negantem non est disputandum (Latin, alternatively Contra principia negantem disputari non potest and Contra principia negantem disputari nequit; literally, "Against one who denies the principles, there can be no debate") is a principle of logic and law: in order to debate reasonably about a disagreement, there must be agreement about the principles or facts by which to judge the arguments.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Contra principia negantem non est disputandum

label: Inference engine
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Inference engine", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the field of artificial intelligence, an inference engine is a software component of an intelligent system that applies logical rules to the knowledge base to deduce new information.

label: Functional fixedness
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Functional fixedness", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias that limits a person to use an object only in the way it is traditionally used.

label: Deliberative indispensability argument
summary: English Wikipedia (article "Deliberative indispensability argument", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The deliberative indispensability argument is an argument for normative realism defended by David Enoch, most prominently in his 2011 book Taking Morality Seriously.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Deliberative indispensability argument

label: Catuṣkoṭi
